title: Meeting Someone --- Welcome, Greeting, Hug, Smile, Guest

lessons.title: bienvenido — well come, in two words you already have
lessons.gloss: welcome — bien plus venido, well come, two pieces you already own

segments.text: What did sucidus describe before it meant dirty? (Unwashed wool, still greasy.) Now a word with nothing new in it but the joining.
bien — well, and the first half of this word.
hola — the greeting you have opened with since the start.
bien-ve-NI-do, stress on the ni. The v is the same soft sound you give b — two letters, one sound. see reference.
bienvenido — "welcome."
Two pieces, both of them plain. bien, well, which you have; and venido, come, the participle of venir. Latin put it the same way round: bene venutus, well come.

English welcome looks like the identical build and is not one. Old English had wilcuma, from willa, desire, and cuma, a comer: the person you wanted to arrive. Norse and French pressure then bent wil- into wel-, and the word ended up resembling "well" plus "come" by accident.
So two languages reached the same shape from opposite directions. Spanish means it literally. English only appears to.
Nothing here was new except the joining.
Bien you had already, and venido has venir audible inside it. A compound you can take apart is a word you do not have to memorise — and Spanish builds a great many of its politest words this way.

segments.instruction: the two pieces on their own — bien, venido
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the two pieces on their own — *bien*, *venido*]

segments.instruction: hola, then bienvenido, as you would at a door
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *hola*, then *bienvenido*, as you would at a door]

segments.text: What are the two pieces of bienvenido? (Bien and venido.) Is English welcome built the same way? (No — it was wilcuma, a desired comer.)

lessons.title: el saludo — a wish for your health, worn smooth
lessons.gloss: a greeting — from salutem, health: to greet was to wish someone their health

segments.text: Before the new one: what are the two pieces of bienvenido? (Bien and venido.)
bienvenido — what you say; this is what you are doing.
hola — one particular instance of it.
sa-LU-do, stress on the lu. The d between two vowels is soft, closer to the th of English this than to a hard d. see reference.
el saludo — "a greeting."

From saludar, to greet, and behind that Latin salutem, health — the accusative of salus, soundness and safety. To greet a Roman was to wish him his health, and Spanish still raises a glass with salud and answers a sneeze with it.
English took the same Latin word more than once. Salute is the soldier's version, borrowed whole. Salutary and salubrious kept the health and dropped the greeting altogether.
So a saludo is not really a word. It is a wish, repeated until nobody hears it any more — which is what centuries do to every polite formula, in every language.
You have been greeting people since your first lesson without a name for the act.
This is the name. Having one lets you talk about the thing rather than only do it — and that is a step up in what you can say.

segments.instruction: bienvenido and then el saludo — the word, then the act
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *bienvenido* and then *el saludo* — the word, then the act]

segments.text: What is behind saludo? (Salutem, health.) Which English word is the soldier's version of it? (Salute.)

lessons.title: el abrazo — the arm is still inside the word
lessons.gloss: a hug — from bracchium, the arm: the word says what the body does

segments.text: Before the new one: what did saludo wish you? (Your health.)
la mano — a part of the body you already have.
el saludo — the greeting this one belongs to.
a-BRA-zo, stress in the middle. The r is a single tap, and the z is the th of think in much of Spain and an s elsewhere. see reference.
el abrazo — "a hug."

From abrazar, and inside it Latin bracchium, the arm: ad-bracchiare, to put your arms around. The word says exactly what the body does, and Spanish never hid it — brazo is still the word for the arm itself.
English embrace is the same build through French, in plus bracchium. A bracelet is a little arm-band. A brace holds a thing the way an arm holds it.

Latin took bracchium from Greek brakhion, which meant the shorter upper arm — from brakhys, short, the same brachy- that turns up in a scientist's vocabulary. The hug goes back to a word for shortness.
Three words now, and each of them is something you could point at.
A welcome, a greeting, an embrace. None of the three needed grammar to be useful — which is worth remembering when a language starts to feel like rules.

segments.instruction: un abrazo, which is how a letter ends
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *un abrazo*, which is how a letter ends]

segments.instruction: el saludo and el abrazo one after the other
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *el saludo* and *el abrazo* one after the other]

segments.text: What is inside abrazo? (Bracchium, the arm.) Which English word is the same build? (Embrace.)

lessons.title: la sonrisa — a laugh with the volume down
lessons.gloss: a smile — subridere, to laugh slightly: a laugh with the volume turned down

segments.text: Before the new one: what is inside abrazo? (Bracchium, the arm.)
el abrazo — the last one, and another thing a face or a body does.
bien — well, which you have had since the beginning.
son-RI-sa, stress on the ri. The s is clear and never buzzes into a z sound the way an English s between vowels does. see reference.
la sonrisa — "a smile."
From sonreír, and that is Latin subridere: sub-, under or slightly, plus ridere, to laugh. A smile is a laugh with the volume turned down. The sub- wore to son- on the way in.
English keeps ridere only at the loud end, and only in loans: to deride is to laugh at, ridicule is the laughing itself, and something risible is worth a laugh.
So Spanish built its quiet word out of the noisy one by putting sub- in front. English never built it at all — smile is Germanic and has no Latin in it.
Sub- is a dial, not a word.
Under, slightly, a little less than the whole thing. Once you can hear it, a long Latin word stops being one item to memorise and becomes two smaller ones you can already handle.

segments.instruction: el abrazo and la sonrisa, one after the other
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *el abrazo* and *la sonrisa*, one after the other]

segments.text: What does sub- do to ridere? (Turns the laugh down to a smile.) Which English words kept the laughing? (Deride, ridicule, risible.)

lessons.title: el invitado — named by what was done to him
lessons.gloss: a guest — the invited one; Spanish names the person by what was done to him

segments.text: Before the last of the five: what does sub- do to ridere? (Turns the laugh down to a smile.) And what is inside abrazo? (The arm.)
el abrazo — what you might give this person.
la sonrisa — and what you would give with it.
in-vi-TA-do, stress on the ta. Four syllables, all of them short and even; Spanish does not swallow the unstressed ones the way English does. see reference.
el invitado — "a guest."
From invitar, Latin invitare, to invite. Invitado is its participle, "invited" — so Spanish names the guest by what was done to him, exactly as bienvenido names a welcome by what is wished.
Put the two side by side. venido in the first of these five and invitado in the last are the same piece of grammar doing the same job: an action turned into a description of a person.

English guest is a different word altogether, Germanic gastiz — which is also the source of Latin hostis, a stranger and then an enemy. Two peoples had one word for the man at the door and could not agree whether he was a visitor or a threat.
Five, and the run is closed: bienvenido, el saludo, el abrazo, la sonrisa, el invitado.

Two of the five are participles, and that is the pattern worth carrying forward. Spanish is unusually willing to name a person or a thing by an action already finished — the one invited, the one welcomed — and once you notice it you will find it everywhere.

segments.instruction: all five in order — bienvenido, el saludo, el abrazo, la sonrisa, el invitado
segments.source: [YOU SAY: all five in order — *bienvenido*, *el saludo*, *el abrazo*, *la sonrisa*, *el invitado*]

segments.instruction: the two participles on their own — bienvenido, invitado
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the two participles on their own — *bienvenido*, *invitado*]

segments.text: What is an invitado, literally? (One who has been invited.) Which other word in this run is a participle? (Bienvenido — well come.) And what did saludo wish you? (Your health.)
